title: The screen pass: letting the pass rush in on purpose
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this morning: still one logged game (Eagles at Bears, Week 3, 0 saved snaps), no review files, last updated Oct 12; the original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable from this run (access denied: not configured for this session). So there's no miss of yours to fix yet. This lesson picks up Sunday night: Seattle's pass rush held Kansas City to 4.3 yards a play and no red-zone trips, and the play offenses use to punish a rush like that, the screen, scored the longest TD of Denver's win at Arizona. It's also the play most likely to fool you in the drill (it starts as a pass and ends looking like a run).

The big idea: most pass plays try to keep the rushers away from the quarterback. A screen does the opposite: the blockers let the rushers in on purpose, then slip out in front of a running back (or receiver) who catches a short pass behind the line. The defenders who were chasing the quarterback are now behind the play, and the ball carrier has blockers in front of him in open space.

White = offense, yellow = defense. Numbers match the steps below. The ghost circle is where the quarterback started.

  1. The quarterback sells a deep pass (1). He drops back 7 yards, as if waiting for a long route. The deeper he goes, the farther the rushers run, and the more of them end up behind the play.
  2. The linemen let the rushers through, then release (2). The center, right guard and right tackle block for about a count ("one-thousand-one"), let their man go, and run sideways to the flat. That's the tell for a defender: a lineman who stops pushing. Against a team that rushes hard every snap, like Seattle (No. 1 in ESPN's pass-rush win rate), that's exactly the habit a screen uses.
  3. The short throw, behind the line (3). The quarterback lofts the ball over the rushers to the back, who has drifted out to the side. Because the pass is caught behind the line of scrimmage, the linemen are allowed downfield: the "ineligible man downfield" rule (1 yard in the NFL, 3 in college; Lesson 35) only applies to passes thrown beyond the line.
  4. The back follows his blockers (4). Three big linemen against a linebacker and a cornerback in open space: that's how a 2-yard throw becomes a long gain. Sunday at Arizona, Denver's RJ Harvey took a short screen 52 yards for a touchdown (20-6, 3rd quarter); it came on a day both defenses were attacking upfield (Denver's own rush hit Jacoby Brissett 12 times), the kind of game where a screen finds open grass.
  5. Other screens: the bubble (a slot receiver steps back and catches a quick lateral throw while the outside receiver blocks), the tunnel (a receiver cuts inside behind linemen who block outward), and the tight-end screen. All work the same way: give the defense the space it's rushing into, then use it.
  6. Why the Chiefs couldn't fix Sunday night with it. A screen needs the rushers to over-commit. Seattle's linemen won one-on-one without blitzing, and its linebackers stayed home (rookie Nick Emmanwori had 2 pressures and forced the interception while covering). Kansas City finished with 213 yards. When a defense rushes four and covers with seven, there's no empty space for a screen to use. That's the counter to the counter.
  7. For your bets. Screens are why running-back receiving props and "longest reception" props can surprise: one screen can be 50 yards. A team facing a strong pass rush with a backup quarterback (Philadelphia Monday night, with Tanner McKee against Dallas) will throw screens to its back to keep the rush honest, which adds catches but rarely adds carries.

How to log it in your drill: a screen is a PASS, even though it ends with a running back running behind blockers. Pre-snap clues: 2nd- or 3rd-and-long (6+ yards); the back in the shotgun beside the quarterback; the defense showing blitz (linebackers walked up to the line). If you see those together, PASS is the safe call, and a screen is one of the reasons. After the snap, watch the linemen: if they stop pushing and run sideways, it's a screen. When the drill scores it, a screen counts as a pass; if you called RUN because the result looked like a run, that's the play doing its job.

Real examples to look for: Monday night, Cowboys at Eagles (Tue 9:15 a.m. JST / Mon 5:15 p.m. PT, ESPN/ABC): watch for Philadelphia screens to Saquon Barkley on 2nd-and-long. Thursday, Panthers at Packers (Fri 9:15 a.m. JST / Thu 5:15 p.m. PT, Prime Video). Saturday in college, Ohio State at USC (Sun 8:30 a.m. JST / Sat 4:30 p.m. PT, NBC): spread offenses run bubble screens almost every series.

Video: search YouTube for "RJ Harvey screen touchdown Cardinals," "running back screen pass explained," and "bubble screen vs tunnel screen."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 5: Plays)

quiz.q: On a screen pass, what do the offensive linemen do?
o: Block their men as long as possible
Block for about a count, let the rushers go, then run to the flat to block downfield
Drop back to protect the quarterback
quiz.w: They let the rushers through on purpose, then release sideways to lead the ball carrier. A lineman who stops pushing is the tell.

quiz.q: Why are linemen allowed downfield on a screen but not on a halfback pass?
o: The screen pass is caught behind the line of scrimmage, and the ineligible-downfield rule only applies to passes thrown beyond it
Referees don't watch linemen on screens
quiz.w: The rule (1 yard NFL, 3 college) only applies to forward passes that cross the line. A screen is thrown behind it.

quiz.q: It's 3rd-and-9, the back is beside the quarterback in the shotgun, and two linebackers walk up to the line showing blitz. Your drill call?
quiz.w: Long yardage, shotgun, blitz look: PASS. A screen is one of the most likely calls against a blitz, and it counts as a pass even if it looks like a run afterward.

quiz.q: Why didn't screens rescue Kansas City against Seattle on Sunday night?
o: The Chiefs never tried a pass
Seattle won with four rushers and kept its linebackers back in coverage, so there was no empty space for a screen
Screens are illegal in prime time
quiz.w: A screen needs rushers to over-commit and leave space. Seattle rushed four, won one-on-one, and covered with seven: KC finished with 213 yards and no red-zone trips.
